variants.name: Typed p-retry wrapper
variants.idiom_name: pRetry<T>(fn, options) with typed options and AbortError classification
variants.implementation_notes: TypeScript adds types to the same promise wrapper: pRetry<T> returns Promise<T>, the options object is typed ({ retries, factor, minTimeout, maxTimeout, randomize, maxRetryTime, signal, shouldRetry, onFailedAttempt }), and AbortError is the typed way to mark a permanent failure (a 404) without writing a classification callback. randomize multiplies each computed timeout by a factor between 1 and 2 and maxRetryTime is measured with a monotonic clock, so the budget survives wall-clock adjustments; the signal option binds the loop to an AbortSignal. The typed policy object is the reason to prefer this over a hand-rolled loop in application code.
pitfalls: The defaults are 10 retries with maxTimeout Infinity: a failing dependency is retried ten times with unbounded growth unless both are set.
p-retry aborts on most TypeErrors (network errors excepted), so a programming bug wrapped in a retryable error class gets retried.
The loop aborts through signal, but each attempt must pass the same signal to fetch, or an abandoned request keeps running after the retry loop has stopped.

variants.name: AWS SDK standard retry mode (full jitter + retry quota)
variants.idiom_name: typed client config (maxAttempts, retry_mode) over the SDK's standard retry strategy
variants.implementation_notes: When the dependency is an AWS service, the typed client configuration selects a schedule the SDK executes: the standard retry mode (documented default) computes delay = random(0,1) x min(20 s, base_delay x 2^retry) - full jitter, with a 50 ms base for transient errors and a 1 s base for throttling - honours a server-directed x-amz-retry-after without extra jitter, and guards retries with a quota token bucket so service-wide failures are not amplified. The configuration is declarative (max_attempts, retry_mode through client config, environment variables or the shared config file), which keeps the schedule out of application code; the remaining design work is marking non-idempotent operations and choosing the total request budget.
pitfalls: The retry quota is per client instance and quietly stops retrying when failures are widespread, so the final error does not reveal whether retries happened.
Adaptive mode can delay the initial request, not just retries, which changes the latency profile of a call that was never expected to wait.
